title: From quantum emitters to technological platforms: a perspective on semiconductor quantum dots
authors: Klaus D. Jöns, Dorian A. Gangloff, Doris E. Reiter
abstract: Photonic quantum technologies are based on controlled photon states. To generate these, quantum dots have emerged as excellent sources of single and entangled photons. In this Perspective, we briefly review the chronological development of quantum dots as photon sources, from their beginnings as quantum emitters in the early 2000s to the advanced photonic devices being developed today. We highlight the interplay between fundamental research and industrial aspects before discussing the photonic quantum technologies we expect to emerge in the near future.
summary: This perspective reviews the maturation of semiconductor quantum dots as sources for quantum light, detailing the progress from initial single-photon demonstrations to complex entangled sources. It highlights the critical interplay between fundamental physics breakthroughs (spin control, coherence engineering) and engineering challenges (telecom compatibility, integration). The paper argues that the field is moving toward realizing fully integrated, scalable quantum photonic hardware.
main_problem: The central challenge is developing robust, scalable, and high-fidelity sources of single and entangled photons from semiconductor quantum dots to power photonic quantum technologies.
main_result: The field has progressed from basic single-photon emission demonstrations to advanced control over spin and photon states, pushing towards deterministic, telecom-compatible, and integrated quantum devices.
method: The review synthesizes decades of research, covering experimental advancements in QD growth and optical characterization alongside theoretical modeling of light-matter and spin dynamics.
model_or_system: The primary system is the semiconductor quantum dot (QD) in III-V materials, which acts as a coherent light-matter interface. Theoretical models incorporate electron-phonon coupling, hyperfine interactions, and are evolving from simple Jaynes-Cummings models to complex polaron master equations.
key_observables: Single-photon emission rate, indistinguishability, entanglement fidelity, spin coherence time ($T_2^*$), and emission wavelength compatibility (O-band/C-band).
important_parameters: The key constraints involve achieving high determinism, low Fine-Structure Splitting (FSS), and maintaining coherence at telecom wavelengths.
main_assumptions: The review implicitly assumes the successful integration of fundamental quantum control (spin/photon) with scalable semiconductor fabrication techniques.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the chronological evolution of QD research across optics, growth, theory, and spin. Other figures map the feedback loop between fundamental research and industrial application, and the future evolution along performance and scaling axes.
paper_structure: The paper follows a historical and thematic review, tracing the development of QDs across four axes (optics, growth, spin, theory) from the early 2000s to current multi-photon and networking concepts, concluding with future integration challenges.
why_interesting: This is highly relevant as it bridges solid-state physics, open quantum systems (phonon coupling, decoherence), and quantum optics. The detailed discussion of Hamiltonian extensions (beyond simple Jaynes-Cummings) and the interplay between material science (growth) and quantum control is valuable.
